implementation_notes: The C++ baseline hand-rolls the dispatcher over the standard concurrency library: one queue guarded by std::mutex, N std::thread workers waiting on std::condition_variable with a predicate, and a submit() that pushes and notify_one(). What replaces the classic structure is std::condition_variable itself - the wait/notify pair is the hand-off - while Boost.Asio's thread_pool plus boost::asio::post() supplies a ready-made dispatcher and std::jthread (C++20) removes the join bookkeeping and adds cooperative cancellation. Keep the hand-rolled form when the dispatch policy must inspect each message before assignment or when the project cannot take Boost.
pitfalls: Work performed while holding the queue mutex serializes all performers and defeats the pattern; copy or move the message out, then release the lock.
Forgetting notify_all() (or the done flag) on shutdown leaves workers blocked forever in wait(); std::thread destruction without join() terminates the process.
std::condition_variable must be used with std::unique_lock and re-checked with a predicate; a bare wait() callback cannot see spurious wakeups or lost notifications.
The queue's lifetime must outlive all workers - joining before destruction is mandatory, otherwise workers touch a destroyed mutex.

variants.name: Boost.Asio thread_pool with post()/executor hand-off
variants.implementation_notes: Boost.Asio ships the dispatcher: boost::asio::thread_pool is an execution context with a fixed number of threads, boost::asio::post(pool, fn) is the submit step that queues a message for exactly one free thread, and pool.join()/pool.wait() are the shutdown contract. executor_type lets the dispatcher pass "where to run" to collaborators instead of hard-coding a pool. Choose it when the application already uses Asio for I/O or when the dispatch policy can be expressed as scheduling (strands for per-key serialization) rather than message inspection.
pitfalls: post() on a stopped or joined pool silently drops the work; stop accepting new messages before join().

Task lifetime is your responsibility: the posted functor and everything it captures must stay alive until the handler runs - capture by value or use shared ownership, never a reference to a stack object.
A single Asio strand serializes its tasks; posting a whole workload to one strand recreates a single-performer pipeline, which may be intended (ordering) but is not parallelism.
Blocking inside a pool thread starves the other tasks scheduled on that thread; blocking work needs its own pool or Asio's dedicated blocking facilities.

variants.name: C++20 std::jthread workers with cooperative stop tokens
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 std::jthread makes the pool's lifecycle automatic - destruction requests a stop and joins - and gives every worker a std::stop_token so shutdown can interrupt a waiting dispatcher or worker without a separate done flag. The queue and hand-off stay the same as the classic form; what changes is the cancellation contract: wait on the condition variable with an interruptible predicate (condition_variable_any::wait with the stop token) and check stop_requested() before long-running message processing. Choose it when the toolchain is C++20 and deterministic shutdown of a long-lived dispatcher matters.
pitfalls: The stop token only sets a flag: a worker that never checks stop_requested() (or never waits on the token) still runs to completion, so shutdown timeouts must be enforced by the dispatcher.
condition_variable_any works with std::stop_token but is slower than std::condition_variable; mixing the two in one queue deadlocks the stop-aware waiters (notify_all on the wrong object).
std::jthread auto-joins on destruction, so a pool member that blocks forever makes destruction (and therefore process exit) hang; stop request plus notify are both required.
Stop tokens are not broadcast automatically: request_stop() on one worker does not stop the others, and the dispatcher must notify every waiter.
